title: Chez Florence and the tip-splitting singers' band
summary: At a gangster-run Chez Florence the six-piece band was incidental to singer Kid Snead and others, and the club closed after the boss broke a patron's nose.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Then what happened after that? Club Alabam. Then I got another job when the Club Alabam closed; I went into the Chez Paree...Chez Something... It was some woman's name. It was supposed to be her club. It was really operated by Texas Guinan's brother -- he was a gangster.
[PAUSE]

Yeah, it was run by Texas Guinan's brother. Texas Guinan at that time was a really big woman in New York. She was a big star, you know. And he was nothing but... He was a gangster. Well, they had this club, and it had just opened up. Chez Florence was the name of the club. How could I forget that name? That's my mother's name, my sister's name, my niece's name.
Chez Florence.
I should know the name. Florence. Anyway, Chez Florence was the name of the club, and it opened up... Big-time club...
Downtown?
Yeah. I forget what street it was. But it was a fine place, and they catered to nothin' but the hoi polloi. We went to work at eleven o'clock at night, and we
Holmes (10/9) - 65
didn't get through until three in the morning.
And what kind of band?

Well, it was mostly... The band was incidental. It was mostly entertainers. There were singers. We had a fellow there who did show numbers and things that people liked -- I mean, those Society people. Anything they named, he could sing it. His name was Kid Snead. And boy, he knew all of the numbers from Europe... You know how Bobby Short is today?
Yes.

That's how he was in them days. He could sing any of them numbers. Oh, he was a big attraction. Because people would like to come in from the shows and things, and they'd want to hear different numbers -- he could sing them.

Well, he was a big attraction. Then they had a couple of women there, singers... Singing was the big thing. Then there was something in the band at times; it was one of them kind of bands, you know. Music didn't mean nothin'.
What size was the band?
Oh, just about six pieces.
Anybody famous in the band?
No. Nobody but me. And I wasn't famous.
Not yet.
Holmes (10/9) - 66

Because I couldn't sing. I was there on a pension. Because I didn't sing. Everything was singing. And they would sing, and go right on to the next standard, or go out on the floor, but while they're singing, we're doing nothing, absolutely nothing. And they go up there, and some of them stayed up there for an hour. As long as the people would give them the money, they'd stay up there and sing. And we were doing nothing.
Somebody had to accompany them, though, didn't they?
Yeah, the piano.
Just the piano.

Yeah, and maybe the drums. But there was nothing for the band. The music didn't mean nothin'. And they would sing-sing-sing and put all the money in one box, and split that at the end of the night. Well, the first night we split up about ten dollars apiece; that was the first night. Of course, it had just opened; there was only a few people in there. And then the next night, the tips was around I think about eighteen dollars, I guess. Getting better. And it was getting better and better.

And what happened? The money's getting big now. Boom! The boss of the place, he gets drunk, and it's a couple in there, a millionaire from Boston... No, the woman is the millionaire, and she was with this guy there. And anyway,
Holmes (10/9) - 67

Tommy, Tommy Guinan, the boss, he's drunk, and messing with this woman, he gets in an argument with the man, and she tells Tommy to shut up, and he hits her in the nose and breaks her nose. Well, this was the first week the club opened up -- the first few days. I think we made two weeks in there, in the club, because that was it. Her daddy put so much weight on for hitting his daughter, and he was a millionaire, too...and just closed the place down. I don't know what happened to Tommy. I don't know if he went to jail or what. But the place closed up, folded up.

All these good jobs... Funny thing, I went from one job right to another. I never had a day off in between. So I don't know if this is the time Willie Lynch come up with this band idea or not. I know I was open, and I took whatever was open to me.
